title: India's Medical Seat Mafia Under Fire as Courts Target NRI Quota Fraud
excerpt: The Supreme Court has declared the NRI quota system in medical admissions 'nothing but a fraud,' as investigations expose an alleged underground network selling MBBS seats for up to ₹4 crore.
body:
• The Supreme Court dismissed Punjab's attempt to expand NRI quota eligibility to distant relatives, calling the system "a money-spinning machine" and "blatantly illegal."
  • Investigations allege medical seats are being sold for ₹1 crore to ₹4 crore through counselling manipulation, forged NRI documents, and fake EWS income certificates.
  • Several deemed universities, including SRM, have abolished their NRI quota following NMC directives, shifting seats to merit-based general counselling.
  • In May 2026, Delhi Police dismantled an inter-state NEET cheating ring that charged parents ₹20-30 lakh per student, rescuing 18 students hours before the exam.

India's medical education system is confronting what investigators and courts describe as an entrenched admission racket — a network of intermediaries, private institutions, and forged paperwork that has allegedly turned MBBS and postgraduate seats into commodities worth crores of rupees.

The Supreme Court has led the charge. In a landmark ruling, a bench of then-Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud and Justices J.B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra dismissed Punjab's appeal against a high court verdict that quashed the state's expansion of NRI quota eligibility to include distant relatives — uncles, aunts, grandparents, and cousins — of non-resident Indians.

"This is nothing but a money-spinning machine. This NRI business is nothing but a fraud. We will put an end to all this."

— Supreme Court bench, dismissing Punjab's NRI quota expansion

How the Alleged Seat Mafia Operates

At the center of the crisis is a practice investigators call "topper blocking." According to multiple investigative reports, agents recruit high-ranking NEET candidates to temporarily occupy seats in private colleges during counselling rounds, even when those students already hold government college placements. Once official rounds conclude, the candidate surrenders the private seat, which reverts to the institution rather than passing to the next eligible student.

The institution then allegedly exercises discretionary control over these returned seats. Investigators in Telangana and Karnataka have uncovered operations involving hundreds of crores, with individual seats reportedly sold for ₹1 crore to ₹4 crore depending on the specialty and institution.

NRI Quota and EWS Fraud

The NRI quota, which reserves roughly 15% of seats in some states for non-resident candidates at higher fee levels, has become a particular flashpoint. Investigative findings cited in court proceedings describe fabricated sponsorship certificates, forged residency records, and the use of intermediaries to secure admission for candidates with no genuine NRI eligibility.

Punjab alone has about 185 NRI quota seats across its medical and dental colleges. The state's attempt to broaden the definition drew sharp rebuke from the court, which noted that candidates with "three times higher marks" were losing seats to quota beneficiaries' distant relatives.

The Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) quota faces parallel abuse. Investigators allege that fake income certificates have enabled affluent families to claim seats reserved for financially disadvantaged students, with certain postgraduate EWS seats reportedly sold for several crores.

Regulatory Gaps at the NMC

The National Medical Commission, India's medical education regulator, has itself come under scrutiny. CBI investigations have surfaced allegations that inspection schedules were leaked in advance, allowing institutions to hire temporary faculty, arrange fake patients, and fill infrastructure gaps only on inspection days.

In response to mounting evidence of abuse, the NMC in 2024 directed deemed universities to review their NRI seat policies. Several prominent institutions, including SRM Institute of Science and Technology in Tamil Nadu, subsequently abolished their NRI quota entirely, moving those seats into merit-based general counselling starting from the 2025 admission session.

A 2026 Crackdown

The problem extends beyond quotas. In May 2026, Delhi Police's Crime Branch dismantled an inter-state NEET cheating ring just hours before the exam. Acting on a tip from Surat Police, officers raided locations across NCR and found 18 students — including minors — held in a Ghaziabad flat under the pretext of studying "leaked" question papers.

The ring, led by a Bihar-based pathology lab operator, charged parents between ₹20 lakh and ₹30 lakh per student, according to police. Four arrests were made across Bihar, Gujarat, and Uttar Pradesh. The rescued students were permitted to sit for the NEET UG 2026 exam as victims of fraud.

"A medical seat in a government institution is not merely an individual gain for a private candidate, but is also a precious resource for our nation that is held in public trust by the regulatory authorities."

— Supreme Court, April 2026

What Comes Next

The Supreme Court has pushed for structural reforms: a unified national counselling mechanism to prevent seat blocking, digital verification of NRI and EWS eligibility through government databases, and stricter penalties for admission fraud. In April 2026, the court reinforced its stance, ruling that medical seats vacated due to fraud must be restored to the next eligible candidate rather than left empty.

For the Indian diaspora, the implications are direct. Legitimate NRI families seeking medical education for their children in India face a system clouded by fraud allegations, while the tightening of quota rules could mean fewer — but fairer — pathways into Indian medical colleges. The court's message is clear: merit, not money, must determine who becomes a doctor.
